TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
WEDNESDAY, 8 MARCH 2023 AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
DAY 44
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MR DOUGLAS FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR BORA KAPLAN, for the Commonwealth
MS PHILIPPA KELLY, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes. Ms Berry. I will just take the appearances for the day.
MS BERRY: Thank you, Commissioner. I appear today in respect of the next witness, with Mr
Freeburn.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear for the Commonwealth with my learned friends
Mr Kaplan and Ms Kelly.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Have you got exhibits you want to tender?
MS BERRY: Yes, Commissioner. May I please tender the exhibits numbered 7075 to 7123 in
today's exhibit list. Those are the exhibits relating to Dr Wurth.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Those items are admitted with the numbers they bear in the schedule.
<EXHIBITS 7075 TO 7123 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
COMMISSIONER: Now, you are calling Dr Wurth. Dr Wurth, I understand you have got a
broken foot and you are better off not on your feet.
DR WURTH: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: So just feel free to remain seated all the time, including when you take the
oath or affirmation. Which is it that you want to take?
DR WURTH: Affirmation, please.
<ELEA WURTH, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MS BERRY
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Berry.
MS BERRY: Thank you, Commissioner. Dr Wurth, can you tell the Commission your full name,
please?
DR WURTH: My full name is Dr Elea Wurth.
COMMISSIONER: Well, "doctor" is not part of your name. Your full name is Elea Wurth.
DR WURTH: Elea Wurth. Yes.
MS BERRY: And, Dr Wurth, you are currently a partner at Deloitte Risk Advisory?

DR WURTH: I am. Correct.
MS BERRY: And is it correct you have been engaged by the Commission to provide expert
advice on aspects of the design and implementation of the Robodebt Scheme?
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.
MS BERRY: And you have prepared a report dated 3 March 2023?
DR WURTH: Yes, that's correct.
MS BERRY: And accompanying end-to-end process maps relating to each program under the
Robodebt Scheme?
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.
MS BERRY: And, Dr Wurth, are the facts stated in your report true and correct to the best of
your knowledge and belief?
DR WURTH: To the best of my knowledge, yes, they are.
MS BERRY: And are the opinions in the report truly held by you?
DR WURTH: They are, yes.
MS BERRY: Dr Wurth, I might just start with some of your qualifications. In your report, you
outline that you are an experienced risk analytics professional?
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.
MS BERRY: And what is your specialisation?
DR WURTH: My specialisation is trustworthy AI and automation.
MS BERRY: And you also describe in your report advanced analytics for enterprise risk and
compliance programs. Are you able to explain a bit about what that involves?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. I have around 20 years' experience in the design, development,
implementation and monitoring of advanced analytics programs, which is machine learning,
artificial intelligence and other techniques, to identify and describe conduct and
non-compliance issues.
MS BERRY: And you hold a PhD from the Australian National University's School of
Regulation and Global Governance?
DR WURTH: I do, yes.

MS BERRY: And what professional memberships do you hold?
DR WURTH: I am a member of the Risk Management Institute of Australasia, I am a fellow of
the Governance Institute of Australia and I'm an affiliate member of the Chartered
Accountants of Australia and New Zealand.
MS BERRY: And, Dr Wurth, is it correct that you have previously worked for the Australian
Taxation Office?
DR WURTH: That's correct. Yes.
MS BERRY: And did you have any involvement with any of the matters that are the subject of
this inquiry?
DR WURTH: No, I did not.
MS BERRY: Dr Wurth, if I can turn then to the documents that you've produced for this
Commission. Is it correct you've provided a series of detailed technical process maps for the
way that data was transmitted between Services Australia, previously known as
DHS - Department of Human Services - and the Australian Taxation Office, and those maps
also include the process by which the data was used at DHS to raise debts.
DR WURTH: Yes, that's correct.
MS BERRY: And you've - the maps that you've produced also identify the changes that
occurred between each of the programs comprising the Robodebt Scheme?
DR WURTH: That's right.
MS BERRY: And by - just to be clear, by "each of the programs comprising the Robodebt
Scheme", you have looked at what was in place prior to Robodebt.
DR WURTH: Yes, that's correct.
MS BERRY: And then you have looked at the PAYG Manual Compliance Intervention program.
Is that - - -
DR WURTH: Yes, that's correct.
MS BERRY: And then you have also then looked at what we know as the OCI, EIC and CUPI
programs?
DR WURTH: Correct. Yes.
MS BERRY: Are you able to describe the process that you followed in order to develop those
maps and your report?

DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. In the development of the maps and the subsequent report that is
based upon those maps, we started - we started from the point of looking to understand the
end-to-end program of Robodebt as a data analytics process. We started from the top, which
was a provision of Statements from the Commission, which include - included Christopher
Birrer, Jeremy Hirschhorn, Tyson Fawcett, Michael Kerr-Brown and Ben Lumley, all of which
had described certain elements of the end-to-end program in differing levels of detail. That
gave us a good sense, or a skeleton if you will, of the end-to-end program right from the
initiation, right through to the interaction with customers.
Once we had that skeleton, each of those Statements then referenced or referred to a
number of other documents which were used to form or support the contents of those
Statements. We then sourced those documents from the Commission that had been
referenced within those documents. And, again, that gave us a greater level of detail and
depth of understanding of that end-to-end process over time. From that point, we assessed
the - our understanding of the end-to-end program and looked to establish where there
were gaps or weaknesses in our understanding and sought additional documentation to be
provided that would help us understand it and really looked for that triangulation, if you will,
from across different sets of documents to establish a level of confidence in each of those
process steps.
MS BERRY: And as part of that process, you describe in your report a hierarchy of
assigned - assumed technical reliability of documents. Are you able to explain that hierarchy
of documents?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. The documents - as you are very aware, there's an enormous
amount of documents that have been made available to the Commission, and they are in
multiple forms and formats. Some of them are reports. Some of them are emails. Some of
them are images and diagrams. What we focused on and really sought to lean on were those
that were - had the highest level of veracity in terms of their technical - well, technical
veracity. So we looked at the documentation that was provided to us and established that
the technical specification documents did appear to have the greatest level of detail, at a
technical level, to really understand the machinations of each step within the program as
they are described. They also were written around the time of implementation, so they had a
timeliness factor to them as well.
So we took the technical specifications as among the top-level confidence documents that
we were looking to refer to. The next level down were technical requirements documents.
These, again, were highly technical in nature and were written around the time of
implementation, so had a timeliness factor. However, a technical requirements document is
more of a - more than a wish list, but it's really looking to describe what's required, which is
then implemented in full or partial form through the specifications. The next level down of
documents that we looked into were - or included and relied upon were Statements that
were made in response to direct requests for information through the Commission, and that
was - that was provided through - through Notices that came through the Commission.
Further down that level of hierarchy and confidence were emails that were exchanged

that time. And then, as I mentioned before, we had started with those Witness Statements,
which were that real description giving the context of the end-to-end process. Whilst we
started with those Witness Statements as to provide that skeleton, we gave them a lower
level of confidence due to the time that had passed between the activities and the provision
of those Statements and the reference - and the requirement to refer to activities that had
happened in the past.
MS BERRY: And, Dr Wurth, just with respect to the first two types of documents you
mentioned - the technical specifications and technical requirements documents - in your
experience, do they require a degree of experience or skill or understanding in order to
properly interpret those kinds of technical documents?
DR WURTH: The technical specifications and requirements - the attempt is to write those in
business language that - that could be interpreted. However, I would say that with a - with
data analytics background and experience is you are much more easily able to interpret and
understand the implications of certain Statements or requirements made.
MS BERRY: Thank you. We might go to your report now. Dr Wurth, you will have a folder on
the desk there in front of you that has some documents I will refer to you, but I can see you
also have a copy - is that a copy of your report that you have in front of you?
DR WURTH: It is, yes.
MS BERRY: And it's already up on the screen. So it is Exhibit 7075, which is
RBD.9999.0001.0451. If we could firstly turn to page 12 of your report and call out figure 1,
which is down towards the bottom of the page. Dr Wurth, can you explain to us just
generally what that figure represents?
DR WURTH: The figure that is being presented here represents the four key phases or stages
of the end-to-end Robodebt program, starting right back in that initial first stage, being
population identification, and then going through those next phases, identity and PAYG data
matching, through income data matching, and then the final stage, which is income data
verification and debt notification, which is the point at which - is the interaction between the
Robodebt system and customers.
MS BERRY: And is it correct that the way you have structured the process maps, they largely
follow the stages outlined in that figure?
DR WURTH: That is correct, yes.
MS BERRY: So if we can start at the start with the population identification stage. If we could
go to page 13 of your report and call out figure 2 at the top of the page. And so is this
correct: this was the point at which DHS would identify the records of the people who would
be selected for data matching with the Australian Taxation Office?
DR WURTH: That is correct, yes.

MS BERRY: Can you take us through what occurred at this stage?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. This is the stage where DHS identified which customers were to
be included within the PAYG matching program. At a very high level, the selection criteria
included receiving a welfare payment or having an outstanding debt to DHS within the
specified year or was partner of a recipient that met one of these criteria within that period.
The - once DHS had identified which customers were to be included within the PAYG
matching program, they created a file which contained all customers that met the criteria;
their customer reference number, which is the unique DHS identifier called a CRN; and a
selection of PII data, personal identifiable information, which includes name, address, date of
birth. Once this file was constructed, that file was passed annually to the ATO.
MS BERRY: And at this - with respect to this stage, did you in your process identify any
differences or changes across the programs comprising Robodebt?
DR WURTH: Yes, I did identify a change. In the pre-Robodebt period, the PAYG manual period
and the OCI period, it was a manual construction of that file by DHS. From 2017, that
changed to - there was a shift to the SAP system which allowed the use of stored procedures
to conduct that process.
MS BERRY: And so can you describe what a manual identification would involve for the
creation of that file prior to 2017?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. Before 2017, a manual construction of that file was dependant on
a data analyst, someone who had access to the DHS systems, to take the requirement and
manually develop that file. So go in, interpret the requirement, construct that file to make
that available for ATO.
MS BERRY: And as I understand what you've said in your report, is this correct: that from
2017, the system that was then used for this extraction allowed that process to be
completed in an automated way?
DR WURTH: I would - I would say semi-automated. I would not consider that to be a fully
automated system. It did allow the storing of certain elements of that process which would
allow it to be more streamlined.
MS BERRY: Alright. And so essentially what you end up with are the records that are then
sent to the ATO?
DR WURTH: Correct. Yes.
MS BERRY: Alright. If we could then go to page 15 of your report and call out figure 3 on that
page. We are now at the second step of that four-stage process. And is this correct: this is
the step at which the exchange between the ATO and DHS occurred?
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.

MS BERRY: Are you able to step us through what happens once the ATO receives those
extract files from DHS?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. On receipt of the extract file from DHS, ATO extracts the
contained information, which is the CRN and the personal identifiable information, and uses
that personal identifiable information provided by DHS to match to a TFN within the ATO. It
is using name, address, date of birth provided by DHS to match to a name, date of birth,
address held by ATO. That's conducted using the CIDC matching engine, which is the Client
Identification Compliance matching engine, to find the potential matches between the two
held datasets.
Once the - there is a match between CRN to TFN, there might be - during that matching
process, a CRN might be matched to multiple TFNs based on different elements of the PII
data. The CIDC engine only retains the highest confidence match of all of the multiple
matches that may have been connected to the CRN. For the list of CRNs matched to TFNs,
there is a reduction of that list to hold only a subset - sorry, I will go back to say that once
the - the CIDC system assigns a match code - a CIDC match code to each of those matches to
describe how it was matched or the type of match that was achieved there, the PAYG system
then retains only a subset of those matches, and they include a subset of high confidence
matches and a subset of medium confidence matches. So the subset of CIDC matches that
are specified within the PAYG program have the - have the PAYG data matched to CRN using
the TFN.
MS BERRY: So you've mentioned a couple of times - it's clear to you that the process that
occurred within the ATO used a person's Tax File Number as part of that process to match
data for people who - whose record had been sent from DHS and who had a client record at
the ATO.
DR WURTH: Correct. Yes.
MS BERRY: And you identified in your report an issue with - you've described the CIDC match
codes, and you've identified in your report what you consider to be an issue with a lack of
control surrounding those match codes. Are you able to explain what your view is with
respect to the confidence levels of the CIDC match codes at this point?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. Within the program protocol, it was specified that only high
confidence matches are used within the PAYG matching program. Through review of the
documentation provided, we established that there was a set of medium confidence
CIDC - medium confidence codes that did have PAYG data matched and provided into the
PAYG system. The lack of control around that - really, there is two elements there. I would
say that the first is the documentation that was provided that described the ATO matching of
PAYG codes included information around a footer file, which is the source of the control
information. When we had a look into the footer file, the content of the footer file was
different to what was described in the documentation to - that described the actual process
of matching that occurred. So this is probably the first step. And the second is a control
conducted on the DHS side on receipt of the matched data, and that is - in the OCI period is

moving into the fuzzy and tight matching controls around provision of confidence - matched
confidence into the system.
MS BERRY: And so I might take us to that point, then. Just to close off on this, essentially
what is demonstrated in that map there is that once - sorry, can you tell me if this is correct:
once the ATO had done their matching process, they removed the Tax File Number from the
record and they then produced a record that was comprised of these - a header file, a footer
file and a PAYG data file, and that's what they sent back to DHS.
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.
MS BERRY: And then what occurred there was that DHS undertook a validation of that data.
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.
MS BERRY: Alright. So can you step us through what occurred when the data was returned to
DHS?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. On return of the - the PAYG population and files through to DHS,
they firstly conducted a validation step around the files received themselves. These are basic
checks around file format, making sure the - you know, things like the file name are correct,
were the header and footer included, were the records contained within the correct length,
are the field formats correct; those kinds of activities. The next step on establishing and
validating the files that had been received was a three-stage identity confirmation process.
MS BERRY: And what were those three stages? Can you take us through those?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. The first stage or step within the identity confirmation was a CRN
validation. So this is a check to ensure that the CRNs that had been passed back from ATO to
DHS were valid according to what was held within the DHS system. So just ensuring that they
matched what was held by DHS records there.
MS BERRY: And, Dr Wurth, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but it might assist - we might bring up
another diagram that shows what you are currently stepping through here. And in the
bundle, which you may have on a trolley beside you, this is in volume 1 at tab 14. It is Exhibit
1121, and it is Document ID CTH.3000.0014.3004_R. And if we could go to page 84 of that
document, which I believe ends in .3087.
DR WURTH: Yes, I have this here.
MS BERRY: If we could go to the next page - I think that's 83. Yes. And if we could call out
that diagram there. Dr Wurth, is this what you're discussing in terms of the matching
processes that are undertaken by DHS once they receive the data back from the ATO?
DR WURTH: That's right, yes.

MS BERRY: And so, sorry, I interrupted you. I think you had just mentioned the CRN
validation, and you were about to move on to the concepts of fuzzy matching and tight
matching.
DR WURTH: That's right. After CRN validation, any CRNs that were not valid were excluded
from the process. Those - for those records where the CRN was validated, it - they went
through a second phase, which is the fuzzy and tight matching process. The fuzzy and tight
matching process each contained a set of rules which were to confirm - which used the same
set of PII data fields - that's the personal identifiable information fields - that's name, address
and date of birth - matching from the ATO provision within the PAYG file to that - what's held
by DHS.
MS BERRY: And so that - is this correct: that links back to what you had identified - the issue
you had identified before, which was for a point in time you found that some of the medium
confidence CIDC codes were being returned to DHS. How does that interact, then, with DHS'
use of these matching techniques?
DR WURTH: When - we did an investigation of the construct of the CIDC match codes, which
is how those match codes or matching occurs within each of those codes, and then tested
that against the rules within the fuzzy and tight ID matching conducted by DHS. What we
established is that of the four medium confidence level matches that were passed from ATO
to DHS, at least three of those would pass through the fuzzy matching system.
MS BERRY: And so ultimately, what outcome does that have for these records in respect of
being included in the Scheme?
DR WURTH: The outcome of these records - or these medium confidence records being
included within the Scheme is that PAYG records that do not have the highest level of
confidence matching to a DHS customer are then being passed into the OCI system.
COMMISSIONER: And in practical terms?
DR WURTH: In practical terms, it means that customers who had PAYG data incorrectly
matched to them would have been included and impacted within the Robodebt Scheme.
MS BERRY: Dr Wurth, I might just take you - I'm sorry, this document isn't in the materials,
but it is a previous exhibit of the Commission. If we might please be able to have up Exhibit
5547, which is Document ID CTH.3000.0009.5841_R. And if we could please go first of all - if
we could have up on the screen both pages 5844 and 5845. And, Dr Wurth, you won't be
familiar with this document, but if you could just assume for the purposes of my questions
that - if we look down the bottom of the page on the left-hand side, there was - these are
emails between DHS staff. And what had occurred was that a customer had contacted them,
and she had advised that she thought there had been a mismatch of data. And if you look
right down the very bottom of the page:
The CUS...

Which I assume refers to customer:
...has advised the following.
And then it set out number 1, and it is - what is redacted there is an employer name and
some amounts. So for two employers down there. And over the top of the page, there is
then - if we could pull that back in. At the top of the next page, there is then - thank
you - another third employer. And you can see there that this person has advised that for
those three employers, they are definitely matched data information not related to her. And
of the five for which - the five employers with which her record was matched, the only two
that belonged to her are then listed underneath. She then said - you can see around halfway
down:
She stated that the three mismatches are employers of her twin sister.
And I appreciate it is redacted and you can't - - -
COMMISSIONER: You don't have an unredacted version you could show Dr Wurth?
MS BERRY: I do, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: And could I just indicate from my friend, what I understood you were
saying, it wasn't a document briefed to Dr Wurth?
MS BERRY: No, it wasn't.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you.
MS BERRY: Dr Wurth, I'm going to provide you with an unredacted version. If you could
refrain from giving those unredacted details out loud in your oral evidence, please. Have you
located where we are?
DR WURTH: Yes, I have.
MS BERRY: Okay. And so this person then stated that she lived at a different address to her
twin sister, and they only have the same last name and birthday. And her sister is not on
Centrelink payments, so she was confused. And then a little bit further down under the
words "annotate by TNX637", there is a note that the Centrelink records were checked, and
the sister's address matches that of the payee address, which are the three mismatches. So,
Dr Wurth, I just wanted to ask you - first of all, this incident appears to have occurred some
time around late 2015. You will see the details were that the letter was sent on the 16th of
July, and then this email is from October in 2015. Can you say what that tells you about the
matching rules that were in place at this point in time?

DR WURTH: For this period of time, this would have been matched using the CIDC matching
engine. And the fuzzy and tight matching confirmation would not have been in place within
DHS at this point.
MS BERRY: So is it correct that all that would have been occurring is that first step of the CRN
validation?
DR WURTH: That's correct. In 2015, yes.
MS BERRY: Are you able to give a view on whether or not the fuzzy and tight matching
processes that were introduced after this point in time would have prevented this from
occurring?
DR WURTH: Yes. Within this, I can see the recipient's name. Do we have the twin's name?
MS BERRY: That's - - -
DR WURTH: We only have that?
MS BERRY: It's redacted, but if you could tell us in general terms what would need to be
matched.
DR WURTH: Certainly.
COMMISSIONER: In the unredacted version, does it appear?
MS BERRY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Just tell Dr Wurth where it appears. She doesn't need to say it out loud, but
she can see what the name is.
MS BERRY: So the initial person's name, Dr Wurth, is on the very first page. There is some
italicised text about halfway down, and it refers to:
Customer (Ms...
And I understand that her name - her first name appears there. Is that correct?
DR WURTH: Yes. Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And then the twin sister, where does she fit?
MS BERRY: And - yes, the twin sister's name is back on page - the page ending in 5845 under
the text:
She stated that the three mismatches are employers of her twin sister.

And then I believe it sets out her twin sister's name and date of birth. Are you able to - - -
DR WURTH: Yes. Thank you for that. Based on that information, and looking at the fuzzy and
tight rules which are applied, it would seem that that would pass through the fuzzy - within
the top sets of fuzzy rules there. If you can see on the next page is there are the rules
specified, and it is - you are looking for a fuzzy surname, fuzzy first name and fuzzy date of
birth, when here you would have a tight match on surname, a tight match on date of birth
and a fuzzy first name.
MS BERRY: And so is the upshot of that that because the medium confidence CIDC codes
were being passed to DHS, even when the fuzzy and tight matching rules were introduced, a
circumstance such as this would not have been prevented by those rules?
DR WURTH: It is possible, yes.
COMMISSIONER: It's not the only twin case we've seen, and I think we have heard of
father/son matches at the same address.
DR WURTH: That is also possible based on the fuzzy matching.
MS BERRY: So you do in your report describe the addition of the fuzzy and tight matching
rules as an “uplift” in the process. Can you explain what you mean by that?
DR WURTH: Certainly. Prior to OCI, there was only the CRN validation. There was no checking
or confirmation against the matches that had been provided by ATO beyond CRN. So in
terms of what was in place prior and implementation of the fuzzy and tight rules, this - this
would be an improvement on that.
MS BERRY: And you also observed one other difference in terms of this part of the process
with respect to those CIDC match codes. Can you explain what that was?
DR WURTH: Do you mean difference over time or - - -
MS BERRY: Yes, I'm just referring - at page 16 of your report, you describe at 6.3.3.1 the
differences that you observed. And we just went through the first one about the introduction
of the fuzzy and tight matching rules. But the second one there, you also observed that in
2019 there was an update to the CIDC match codes. Can you explain what you found there?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. In 2019, there was a change to the ATO match - CIDC matching
process by which the four medium confidence codes which had previously been provided to
DHS were dropped. They were no longer provided from 2019.
MS BERRY: And so from that point, it was only high confidence matches that were being
passed through to DHS. Is that correct?
DR WURTH: Correct. Yes.

COMMISSIONER: This is as late as 2019?
DR WURTH: Yes, that's when we identified that within the documentation.
COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MS BERRY: If we could turn then to the third stage in our four-stage process, and that was
income data matching. If we could please go to page 17 of Dr Wurth's report and call out
figure 4 in the middle of the page. Dr Wurth, is this correct: this is the point at which DHS
internally matched the PAYG information it had received from the ATO with a person's
income information on the system that DHS held itself?
DR WURTH: That's correct, yes.
MS BERRY: Can you take us through this part of the process?
DR WURTH: Yes, certainly. On passing the validation phase in the previous map there for
identity matching, the records came in to the third phase of the PAYG program, which was
the income data matching. And as you've mentioned, that is the matching of the ATO PAYG
data to the DHS-held employment income information. As the records entered into this
phase, there was a mass fraud detection strategy initiated.
MS BERRY: And, Dr Wurth, can I just ask you: is that where all of the customer records went?
DR WURTH: If they had passed through the - the identity validation steps, yes, that is where
they came. That's correct. They came through the income data matching and through the
mass fraud detection strategy.
COMMISSIONER: Where did the name "mass fraud detection strategy" come from, do you
know? Is that what it was actually called in the DHS systems?
DR WURTH: Yes, that's correct. That changed from the BI integrity process, before the OCI
period, to the mass fraud detection strategy under OCI.
COMMISSIONER: Even though this was about identifying discrepancies which might be
entirely explicable between PAYG information and reported income?
DR WURTH: That's correct. It was the name of the process where all of the records came
through for - for potential identification of discrepancy.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Did you see anything that explained the name change?
DR WURTH: No explanation on name change, only a difference in the naming convention
between the two periods.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.

MS BERRY: Thank you, Commissioner. And, Dr Wurth, can I just - on page 18 of your report,
you are going through at this point bullet points with respect to people who were excluded
